doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

title: Nelson Jr.'s mother, family care and racial worries
summary: His mother's dementia, his father caring for his own parents, his son's CNN interview, and fear of being stopped.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: That’s wonderful to hear. And how about yourself? What gets under your collar?

Not much. I’m pretty, I’m challenged right now because I have an 87-year-old mother who lives with me and she’s got dementia. So sometimes, we were up there today and she has not been able to go to church. She’s a big churchgoer. She said, “We’re going to church today?” I says, “No, Mom.” And of course she will ask you that fifty times. So having patience to deal with that is tough. And in her situation she can still dress herself. She can still take baths, she can still do stuff, but it’s just challenging to go through that a lot. And it’s not angry necessarily but this is a lady that graduated from high school when she was 15, graduated from college when she was 19, has two master’s degrees, one in Spanish and one in counseling. But dementia doesn’t care.
Didn’t your mother get multiple degrees also?
Yeah this is — my stepmother did, but my mother, my physical mother did. So that’s who I’m talking about.

So she’s staying with me now and my dad taught me something because he made sure that he was going to take care of his family. He built a house in [inaudible] Missouri for his mom and dad, and he made sure that he, as his success rose that he made sure he took care of them. We were really a pretty close family. So that kind of challenges me a lot. The racial situation challenges me. I have a son who is an attorney and actually this is interesting — when George Floyd was killed one of his clients saw the police and stuff deal with George Floyd before he was murdered. And my son had an interview with Chris Cuomo on CNN. And he was very eloquent and my dad would have been very proud of him to do that kind of stuff. But living as an African-American even at 65 years old, I’m suspect to get stopped at any time.
I mean, and that is awful.
